title: Day and night of Brahma (8.17–8.28)
hook: a single day of the creator lasts a thousand ages, and the universe breathes in and out with it
tomorrow: "I will tell you the most secret" (9.1–9.10)

segments.voice: Yesterday, sulabha: a king who died thinking of a fawn. Your line was what you think at the end. Today, the biggest clock in the Gita, at the end of chapter eight.
screen: `SULABHA — WHAT YOU THINK AT THE END.`

segments.voice: Bhishma, the great elder of the Mahabharata, falls in battle, pierced by so many arrows that his body rests on them like a bed. And he doesn't die. He had been given the power to choose his time. So he lies on the arrows for days, teaching, waiting. Waiting for what? For the sun to turn north: uttarayana, the sun's northern course. Only then, the story says, does he let go. Why would the sun's direction matter at the moment of death? The end of chapter eight is where that idea lives.
screen: `A BED OF ARROWS.` → `BHISHMA WAITS.` → `FOR THE SUN TO TURN NORTH.`

segments.voice: First, the enormous clock. Verse seventeen: those who know that a day of Brahma, the creator, lasts a thousand ages, and his night another thousand, truly know day and night. When Brahma's day dawns, all things come out of the unmanifest; when his night falls, they dissolve back into it. Verse nineteen: the same crowd of beings, born again and again, dissolves helplessly at nightfall and comes forth again at day. The whole universe breathing in and out. But, verse twenty, beyond that unmanifest is another, eternal, which doesn't perish when all beings perish. That's the highest goal; whoever reaches it doesn't return. Then the two paths, verses twenty-four and twenty-five. One: fire, light, day, the bright half of the moon, the six months of the sun's northern course. The knowers of Brahman who go by it reach Brahman. The other: smoke, night, the dark half of the moon, the six months of the southern course. Those who go by it reach the light of the moon, and return. Commentators read this differently. Some take it as the actual timing of death, and Bhishma's waiting fits that reading. Others read the markers as guides or stages on the soul's journey, the path of light and the path of smoke. Verse twenty-seven is clear either way: the yogi who knows these two paths isn't confused. A clock so large it holds the universe, and something beyond it that no clock touches.
screen: `A THOUSAND AGES FOR A DAY.` · `THE UNIVERSE BREATHES IN AND OUT.` · `BEYOND IT, WHAT NEVER PERISHES.` · `THE PATH OF LIGHT, THE PATH OF SMOKE.` · then, large: `THE TWO PATHS.`

segments.voice: Let your breath become a very small version of Brahma's day and night: on the in-breath, let sounds, thoughts and the feel of the room come forth; on the out-breath, let them dissolve back into quiet. In, the world appears; out, it rests. For the last few breaths, notice what doesn't come and go: the awareness watching both.
Uttarayana. The sun's northern course, what Bhishma waited for on his bed of arrows. A thousand ages each: the universe coming forth and dissolving, and beyond it, the eternal that never perishes.
Your line: the two paths. One of light, one of smoke, and the one who knows both isn't confused. Day one hundred eighty-eight, done.

screen: `DAY 188 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: "I WILL TELL YOU THE MOST SECRET."`

howItsDone: Many Hindus consider uttarayana, the sun's northern course marked by the festival of Makar Sankranti, an auspicious time, and the Mahabharata's Bhishma is remembered for waiting for it before he died.

original.note: Sanskrit: uttarayana, the sun's northern course; uttara (north) + ayana (going).

trapdoor: what you thought: a day is a day.
what it means: a day of Brahma is a thousand ages; the universe comes forth and dissolves, and the eternal lies beyond it.

what a scholar hears: 8.24–26 echo the Upanishads' devayana and pitriyana, the path of the gods and of the ancestors; Shankara reads the markers as presiding deities who guide the soul, not calendar times.
